FOREWORD 

This Indian Standard ( First Revision ) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft 
finalized by the Gears Sectional Committee had been approved by the Light Mechanical Engineering 
Division Council. 

This standard was first published in 1967 and an amendment was issued in 1978 to give additional 
information regarding properties of materials recommended for manufacture of cylindrical gears. This 
first revision has been issued to align the standard with the International practices taking into account 
the work done by ISO technical committee ISO/TC 60 'Gears'. The standard is based on the 
corresponding ISO documents for cylindrical gears and presents the data and calculation formulae in 
more rational manner. 

In line with the International practices for designing of gears, load capacity of cylindrical gears is 
evaluated based on limitation by contact stresses and bending stresses. Accordingly, the revision is 
being presented in three parts so that the standard may be utilised more effectively. The Part 1 
of this standard deals with the introduction, symbols and general influence factors for design of gears. 
Detailed step by step calculation procedures for calculation of load factors taking into account the 
effect of surface durability ( pitting ) is given in Part 2. There is appropriate reference to tables 
and graphs for arriving at various factors. Part 3 covers the calculation procedure for calculating 
the load factors with respect to bending strength. These parts have been presented in such a format 
that the standard may be directly used for arriving at various factors relevant for calculations. In order 
to help the designer, examples of use of the two sections have been included in the Annex A and B 
to the standard. 

The formulae and tables given in this standard apply to the calculation of load capacity of cylindrical 
external gears — spur, helical and double-helical; with peripheral speeds less than 50 m/s. 

IS 9466 : 1980 « Viscosity classification of industrial liquid lubricants' or ISO 3448 : 1975 'Industrial 
liquid lubricants — ISO viscosity classification' may be referred for viscosity grade.

3 GENERAL INFLUENCE FACTORS 
3.1 Application Factor, K A 

The application factor, Ka accounts for dynamic over- 
loads from sources external to the gearing. The over- 
loads depeud on characteristics of driving and driven 
machines, the ratio of masses, the couplings and operat- 
ing conditions. If possible, the application factor should 
be determined by precise measurement or by a com- 
prehensive system analysis. In case neither one of these 
two is practicable, application factor shall be selected 
as per the guidelines furnished in Tables 1, 2 and 3. 
3 X Dynamic Load Factor, K\ 
The dynamic load factor, Ky is defined as the ratio 
between the maximum force which occurs at the mesh 
of an actual gear pair and the corresponding load due 
to the externally applied load. The dynamic load factor 
is mainly influenced by: 

a) transmision errors, 

b) polar moments of inertia of pinion and gear, 

c) mesh stiffness, 

d) transmitted load including application factor, 



e) lubrication, 

f) damping characteristics of the gear system, 

g) shaft and bearing stiffnesses, and 

h) load bearing pattern on tooth flanks. 
Method of calculating the dynamic load factor fur- 
nished in this standard is suitable for: 

1) steel gears of heavy rim section, 

2) gears of average to heavy loading, 

f 
-~>150N/mm 

3) gears involving pinions with relatively small 
numbers of teeth, 

4) Running speed in the sub-critical range: 

For helical gears: v . rgjj < 14 approx 
For spur gears: v . rjgr < 10 approx 

5) All types of gears, if v.-^*< 3

3 3 Longitudinal Load Distribution Factors, K\\\\ 
and X|-p 

The longitudinal load distribution factor, K\^ is to 
account lor the non-uniform distribution ot load across 
the face-width. This depends on the inrsh alignment 
error of the loaded gear pair and the mesh stiffness. The 
main intlucticing factors are: 

a) errors in the manufacture of teeth, 

b) errors in mounting due to bore errors, 

c) bearing allowances, 

d) stiffness of teeth, 

e) stiffness of the gear core, 
stiffness of the housing, 
g) deformation of bearings, 



h) surface irregularities caused by loading, 

j) thermal deformation for high speed gears, 

k) (angcutial and axial loads, 

m) lapping effects, 

n) longitudinal corrections done on the teeth, attd 

p) overhung loads on shafts. 
The factor /C Hp can be analysed by a complete evalua- 
tion of all the. elements of influence, and can be 
inspected, for example, by measuring the stress at the 
tooth root in actual operation or by a critical examina- 
tion of the meshing pattern on the teeth at full load. 

In case, the influencing elements are not sufficiently 
known for a precise calculation of /Chb, the approximate 
method described in this standard can bi » .cJ. 



Longitudinal load distribution factor for bending stress, 
Kf$ enables to take into account the effects of uneven 
distribution of load along the length of the tooth. 
For gears in general mechanical use with the teeth cut 
directly from through hardened steel, the value of ATpa, 
is very close to /fas- But, in case of surface hardened 
teeth, Xfs is marginally less than K^ (about 5%). In 
general, same value can be taken for ifas and Jfrp. 
Formulae for the calculation of Ku$ and £fb are given 
in Table 4. 

3.4 Transverse Load Distribution Factors, K\\ a nod 

A'Fu 

The distribution of the total tangential load on several 
pairs of teeth in contact depends on the dimensions 
given to the gears, the precision and the value of the 
tangential force. Transverse load distribution factor 
takes into account the distribution of actual load during 
the gear mesh. 



IS44*0(Partslto3):1995 

The main influencing factors are: 

a) the overall rigidity of the gear mesh, 

b) the total tangential load, 

c) the base pitch error, 

d) tip relief of the teeth, 

e) face width of the teeth, 

f) influence of lapping, and 

g) the dimensions of the gear. 

As far as general mechanical use is concerned, factor 

#Ha can be selected from Table 5. 

The transverse load distribution factor for bending 

stress, Kf takes into account the effect of transverse 

distribution of loads during the tooth meshing. For the 

gears of general mechanical use, factor Afp« can be 

taken as equal to Xho*

3*9 Life Factor for Contact Stress, Zl 

The life factor, Z L takes into account a higher permis- 
sible Hertzian stress if only limited life is required. 
The main influencing factors are: 

a) material and hardness, 

b) number of cycles, and 

c) factors Zr,Zv,Zl,Zw and Zs. 

The formulae furnished in Table 7 can be used for the 
calculation of Z L .

3.12 Work Hardening Factor for Contact Stress, Z w 

Work hardening factor takes into account the increase 
of surface durability due to meshing of gear with a 
hardened pinion with smooth tooth surfaces. 



IS 4440 (Parts 1 to 3) : 1995 

The increase of surface durability of the soft gear is 
dependent not only on the work-hardening of the soft 
gear but also on the other factors such as alloying 
elements of the soft material, Hertzian stress, hardening 
process and surface roughness of the hard pinion. 
The work hardening effect should be evaluated from 
results of tests or Geld experiences with gears. In the 
absence of such data, the following formula can be used 
for the evaluation of the approximate value of Zw • 

Zw - 1.2 - — ■■' — 
^ 1700 

for 130 < HB < 400, Zw can be taken as unity. 
3.13 Size Factor for Contact Stress, Zs 

The size factor, Z s accounts for the influence of tooth 
dimensions on allowable contact stress. In principle, 
the flank curvature/radius is suitable as dimension for 
the size. However, for surface hardened gears, the 
hardness depth as compared to the tooth size plays 
a role. Further, as larger modules are found for 
larger diameters, the module can be taken as basis for 
-size.

3.1 4 Roughness Factor for Contact Stress, Zr 

The roughness factor, Z R accounts for the influence of 
surface texture of tooth flanks on surface load capacity. 
Depending on the surface condition of the gears, the 
value of Z R csn be selected from Table 10. 

3.15 Reliability Factor, Jfe 

The reliability factor is introduced to allow the design 
of gears with a calculated risk and higher reliability. 

K& = 1 .0, corresponds to a probability of failure 

of one in 100 at the rated losd and required 

life ft** 0.01). 

For some applications, there may be a requirement for 

a greater or a smaller reliability factor. For such cases, 

Kr can be calculated using the following formula: 



LS44*0(Partslto3):1995 

K R - 0.79 -0.105 log (ft) 
Pi - probability of failure. 
3.1* Life Factor for Bending Stress, Fn 
The life factor for bending stress, Fn takes into account 
the case of limited life (3 X 10 s cycles) where a higher 
root stress can be permitted. Tnc main influencing 
factors are: 

a) material and hardness, 

b) number of cycles (required life), and 

c) influence factors F„, Fr and Y$. 

The life factor Fn can be taken $s unity for a required 
life of more than 3 X 10 6 cycles. For other cases, the 
formulae furnished in Table 11 can be used for the 
calculation of Fn- 

3.17 Form Factor for Bending Stress, Fpa 

The tooth form factor, Fr takes into account the 
influence of the tooth form on the nominal bending 
stress for the application of load at the tooth tip. The 
procedure and die formulae for the calculation of tooth 
form factor, Fp a is given in detail in Part 3 of this

standard. The calculation method is based on the dis- 
tance between the contact points of the 30° tangents at 
the root fillet of the tooth profile. 

3.18 Stress Concentration Factor for Bending 
Stress, F K 

The stress concentration factor, V* takes into account 
the conversion of the nominal bending stress to the local 
tooth root stress. Thereby Vk covers the stress increas- 
ing effect of the fillet (notch) and the bending stresses 
arising at the tooth root. A part of the local stress is 
independent of the bending moment arm and as it 
increases, the point of application of load approaches 
the critical tooth root section. 
Therefore, in addition to its dependence on the notch 
radius, the stress correction is also dependent on the 
positioit on the load application, that is, the size of the 
bending moment ami. Yk applies to the application of 
the load at the tooth tip. 

Kk can be calculated as per the procedure given in 
Part 3 of this standard. 

3.19 Contact Ratio Factor for Bending Stress, Y t 

The contact ratio factor Y t is necessary for the deter- 
mination of tooth root stress ofo- With Y tt the conver- 
sion of applied load at the tip, to the decisive point of 
load application is carried out for approximate calcula- 
tion of maximum tooth root stress arising during the 
meshing of the teeth. 
Y t can be calculated from: 

»0.25 + ™ • 



3.20 Helix Angle Factor for Bending Stress, fy 

The helix angle factor Yp takes into account the dif- 
ference between the helical gear and the virtual spur 
gear in the normal section on which the calculation is 
based. Y$ can be calculated as given below: 



* 1-0.25 80 
*0.75 



331 Factor of Notch Sensitivity for Bending Stress, Y n 

Actual reduction of resistance to fatigue due to notch 
sensitivity is often less than the value of the stress 
concentration factor /&• The main influencing 
parameters of notch sensitivity factor are the material, 
heat treatment nnd the rate of loading. 
Two value aspects are to be considered for this coeffi- 
cient. They are: 

— value relative to the endurance limit, and 

— value relative to the static limiting stress. 

In this standard only the value of notch sensitivity factor 
relative to endurance liuiit is considered because the 
number of working cycles for general mechanical use 



are rarely less than 3 x 10 6 cycles. 

The notch sensitivity factor Y n can be determined from 

Table 12 depending on the material condition. 

3.22 Factor of Relative Surface Roughness for 
Bending Stress, Fr 

A fatigue fracture has its origin in a small crack and it 
is evident that the endurance of a test piece would 
diminish in case of a roughly machined surface. For the 
materials very susceptible to concentration of stress, the 
influence of surface condition is more important The 
surface roughness factor enables to take into account 
the influence of profile roughness on the fatigue life of 
the gear. The relative surface roughness factor is the 
ratio between the surface roughness factor of the gear 
to be determined and a test gear. This value can be 
calculated from the formulae given in Table 1 3. 

333 Size Factor for Bending Stress, Fs 

The size factor, F s takes into account the decrease of 
the strength with increasing size (size effect). The main 
influencing factors are: 

a) material and hardness, and 

b) size of the gear. 

Y s as a function of nonnal module and the material can 
be approximately determined from formulae given in 
Table 14. 

3.24 Endurance Limit for the Contact Stress, 

°Hllni 

For a given material o HHm is the limit of repeated 
Hertzian stress which can be permanently endured. The 
value of o H , im for a material can be regarded as the level 
of Hertzian stress which the material will endure 
without damage for at least 50 x 10 6 load cycles. 
The main influencing factors are: 

a) material composition; 

b) mechanical properties; 

c) hardening process, depth of hardened zone, 
hardness gradient; 

d) structure; 

e) residual stresses; and 

f) material cleanliness and defects. 

a HH« can I* established for any material in any condi- 
tion, by running load tests on gears, made of the 
material in question. It is essential that when test results 
or data from service are interpreted, allowances are 
made on the influences on permissible stresses of such 
variables as lubricant viscosity, surface roughness, 
material combination, etc. 

Figures 3 to 7 give fields relative to flank hardness for 
the endurance limits of given material groups, with 
nonnal heat treatment method. These graphs can be 
used, if the requisite data from load tests or service 
conditions are not available. 

The values furnished in Fig. 3 to 7 correspond to a 
failure probability of 0.01. 



12 



The selection of fatigue strength values at the upper 
limits of the fields demands a special consideration to 
the selection, testing and heat treatment of the material 
and the corresponding control processes. 

Normally the choice of endurance limits is from the 
middle of the fields. 

The endurance limits for Hertzian stress shown in the 
diagrams are valid for:

the material on the tooth root stress which can be 
permanently endured. For steels, the endurance limit is

Boreao of Indian Standards 

BIS is a statutory institution established under tbe Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 1986 to promote 
harmonious development of the activities of standardization, marking and quality certification of goods 
and attending to connected matters in the country. 

Copyright 

MS has the copyright of all its publications. No part of these publications may be reproduced in any 
form without the prior permission in writing of BIS. This does not preclude the free use, in the course 
of implementing the standard, of necessary details, such as symbols and sizes, type or grade 
designations. Enquiries relating to copyright be addressed -to the Director ( Publications ), BIS. 

Review of Indian Standards 

Amendments are issued to standards as the need arises on the basis of comments. Standards are also 
reviewed periodically; a standard along with amendments is reaffirmed when such review indicates that 
no changes are needed; if the review indicates that changes are needed, it is taken up for revision. 
Users of Indian Standards should ascertain that they are in possession of the latest amendments or 
edition. 

This Indian Standard has been developed from Doc No: LM 13 (4461)
